account: Dung 1995 supplies exactly the formal vocabulary for the 'synthesis competence' node: an argumentation framework AF = (AR, attacks) treats answers as abstract atoms linked by a binary attack relation, with no internal structure, weight, or truth value. Admissibility (a conflict-free set that defends every member against all attackers) is the core rationality constraint; on top of it Dung defines a lattice of semantics with different guarantees: preferred extensions (maximal admissible sets; always at least one exists, but symmetric conflicts like the Nixon diamond yield several, so credulous justification is non-unique), stable extensions (conflict-free sets attacking every outside argument; strictly stronger than preferred and may fail to exist at all), and the grounded extension (least fixed point of the characteristic function F_AF(S) = {A | A acceptable wrt S}; always unique, but can be empty — the skeptical adjudicator may justifiably endorse nothing when two agent answers attack each other symmetrically). Complete extensions bridge the two: every preferred extension is complete, and the grounded extension is the least complete one. The key coincidence result for adjudication design: well-founded frameworks (no infinite attack chains) have exactly one extension that is simultaneously grounded, preferred, and stable — the formal condition under which conflict adjudication is unambiguous. Equally important for the note: the framework deliberately does NOT model evidential weight, attack strength, truth, or probabilistic confidence — Dung himself lists differentiating attack strength as necessary future work. Consequence for the research problem: Dung-style adjudication can tell a synthesizer which set of conflicting agent answers is defensible, but it cannot break symmetric ties (two mutually attacking answers produce two preferred extensions and an empty grounded one); whatever breaks the tie — retrieval of external evidence, in our mechanism — is precisely what the formalism lacks and what retrieval-mediated Q/A supplies. The wave-1 combined Dung+Shapiro packet failed with zero evidence (blocked, 'Exceeded maximum output retries'), so this packet is the sole source for the Dung half.
assumptions: Agent 'answers' in the communication experiment can be treated as abstract arguments and cross-agent contradictions/corrections as attack edges; this mapping is our operationalization, not something Dung sanctions.
The OCR garbling in the extracted text (e.g., 'Fo : P_,PR', 'GE,,,o') does not alter the definitional content; all cited definitions were cross-checked against multiple search hits.

citations.excerpt: an argument is an abstract entity whose role is solely determined by its relations to other arguments. No special attention is paid to the internal structure of the arguments. Definition 2. An argumentation framework is a pair AF = (AR, attacks) where AR is a set of arguments, and attacks is a binary relation on AR

claims.statement: An argumentation framework is AF = (AR, attacks) with attacks ⊆ AR × AR; an argument is 'an abstract entity whose role is solely determined by its relations to other arguments' — the internal structure of arguments (premises, evidence, provenance) is deliberately not modeled (Definition 2, `===== PDF PAGE 6 =====`).

citations.excerpt: Definition 5. A set S of arguments is said to be conflict-free if there are no arguments A and B in S such that A attacks B. ... Definition 6. (1) An argument A is acceptable with respect to a set S of arguments iff for each argument B: if B attacks A then B is attacked by S. (2) A conflict-free set of arguments S is admissible iff each argument in S is acceptable with respect to S.
Lemma 10 (Fundamental Lemma). Let S be an admissible set of arguments and A and A' be arguments which are acceptable with respect to S. Then (1) S' = S ∪ {A} is admissible ...

claims.statement: Admissibility machinery: S is conflict-free iff no two arguments in S attack each other (Def 5, `===== PDF PAGE 6 =====`); A is acceptable wrt S iff every attacker of A is itself attacked by S, and a conflict-free S is admissible iff all its members are acceptable wrt S — i.e., a rational agent's accepted set must defend itself against all attacks (Def 6, `===== PDF PAGE 6 =====`). The Fundamental Lemma (adding an acceptable argument to an admissible set preserves admissibility) and Thm 11 (admissible sets form a complete partial order) follow (`===== PDF PAGE 7 =====`).

citations.excerpt: Definition 7. A preferred extension of an argumentation framework AF is a maximal (with respect to set inclusion) admissible set of AF. ... This argumentation framework has two preferred extensions ... Corollary 12. Every argumentation framework possesses at least one preferred extension.

claims.statement: Preferred extensions are maximal (w.r.t. set inclusion) admissible sets and define the credulous semantics (Def 7, `===== PDF PAGE 7 =====`). Existence is guaranteed — every argumentation framework possesses at least one preferred extension (Cor 12) — but uniqueness is not: the Nixon diamond ({A,B}, {(A,B),(B,A)}) has exactly two preferred extensions, so under symmetric mutual attack between two agents' answers the credulous semantics licenses either conclusion and cannot choose between them (`===== PDF PAGE 7 =====`).

citations.excerpt: Definition 13. A conflict-free set of arguments S is called a stable extension iff S attacks each argument which does not belong to S. ... Lemma 15. Every stable extension is a preferred extension but not vice versa. ... the empty set is a preferred extension of AF which is clearly not stable.

claims.statement: Stable extensions are conflict-free sets that attack every argument outside the set (Def 13, equivalently S = {A | A is not attacked by S}, Lemma 14, `===== PDF PAGE 8 =====`). Every stable extension is preferred but not conversely (Lemma 15: the self-attacking single-argument framework has the empty set as a preferred extension that is not stable), and stable extensions may fail to exist at all — Dung argues such 'anomalies' reflect the modeled world, not a bug, i.e., no adjudication guarantee is available in general (`===== PDF PAGE 8 =====`).

citations.excerpt: Definition 20. The grounded extension of an argumentation framework AF, denoted by GE_AF, is the least fixed point of F_AF. ... Example 22 ... it follows immediately that the grounded extension is empty, i.e. a skeptical reasoner will not include anything.
Theorem 25. (1) Each preferred extension is a complete extension, but not vice versa. (2) The grounded extension is the least (with respect to set inclusion) complete extension.
Theorem 30. Every well-founded argumentation framework has exactly one complete extension which is grounded, preferred and stable.

claims.statement: Grounded (skeptical) semantics: the characteristic function F_AF(S) = {A | A acceptable wrt S} is monotonic, and the grounded extension GE is its least fixed point (Defs 16, 20, `===== PDF PAGE 9 =====`) — hence GE always exists and is unique, but may be empty: in the Nixon diamond 'a skeptical reasoner will not include anything' (Example 22). Complete extensions (admissible sets containing every argument acceptable wrt them, Def 23) link the two poles: each preferred extension is complete and GE is the least complete extension (Thm 25, `===== PDF PAGE 10 =====`). Coincidence condition: well-founded frameworks (no infinite attack sequence A_{i+1} attacks A_i) have exactly one complete extension which is simultaneously grounded, preferred, and stable (Thm 30, `===== PDF PAGE 11 =====`) — the formal condition under which adjudication of conflicting answers is unambiguous.

citations.excerpt: the idea of argumentational reasoning is that a statement is believable if it can be argued successfully against attacking arguments. In other words, whether or not a rational agent believes in a statement depends on whether or not the argument supporting this statement can be successfully defended against the counterarguments.

In general, we expect that the attacks against some arguments may have different strengths, one may be more 'deadly' than the others. So a study of how to differentiate the strength of arguments is necessary.

counterevidence: The 'does not model truth/weight' reading is an absence-of-machinery claim: the paper's Definitions 2-31 contain no weight, probability, or truth-value constructs, and the PDF PAGE 31 passage is the author's own confirmation; it cannot be proven from the text beyond this.
claims.statement: What the framework does NOT model: evidential weight, attack strength, truth, or probabilistic confidence. Justification is purely relational 'external stability' — a statement is believable iff it can be successfully defended against counterarguments (`===== PDF PAGE 3 =====`); arguments carry no internal structure or truth status (Def 2, `===== PDF PAGE 6 =====`); and Dung explicitly concedes that 'the attacks against some arguments may have different strengths... a study of how to differentiate the strength of arguments is necessary' and leaves it to future work (`===== PDF PAGE 31 =====`). No probability, no degrees of belief, no aggregation of independent evidential support: two arguments with identical attack graphs are treated identically regardless of the evidence behind them — so symmetric conflicts between agent answers are formally undecidable inside the framework and must be broken by information the semantics does not represent.

counterevidence: Dung does connect argumentation to logic programming, default logic, autoepistemic logic, and n-person games (Sections 3-4), so the framework is not purely syntax — but these reductions inherit the same attack-graph-only information; none adds evidential weight or truth.

The grounded extension being empty in the Nixon diamond is a feature (skeptical caution), not a defect, from Dung's perspective; using 'empty GE = adjudication failure' in the note is our task-specific interpretation, not Dung's claim.
